summary: A set of summary notes covering the RFCs numbered 900 through 999, as a historical reference. It was replaced by RFC 1000, which covers RFCs 1 through 999.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a short book report on a hundred earlier memos, so you can see what they were about without reading them all.

subtitle: An annotated summary of the contents of RFCs 900 through 999, serving as a reference guide to a hundred RFCs.

tldr.problem: With a hundred RFCs published between 1985 and 1987, readers needed to quickly understand what each RFC was about without reading them all.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 999 provides a one-page summary of each RFC from 900 to 999, listing author, publication date, title, and a short description of the content, organized in reverse numerical order from 999 to 900.
tldr.outcome: This reference document was immediately superseded by RFC 1000, which covered all RFCs from 1 to 999 in one comprehensive index, making RFC 999 obsolete within months.

today: RFC 999 was obsoleted within months by RFC 1000, published in August 1987, which provided a comprehensive index of all RFCs from 1 to 999. RFC 999 is now of historical interest only, documenting the state of the protocol suite in spring 1987.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content: RFC 999 is an annotated list of the 100 RFCs numbered 900 through 999, published in April 1987 by A. Westine and J. Postel. It serves as a status report on these RFCs, providing authors, publication dates, titles, and brief descriptions of each document's content. The document is organized in reverse numerical order, starting with RFC 999 itself and working backward to RFC 900. This summary document is distributed without restriction and is designed to help readers quickly identify which RFCs in this range are relevant to their interests without having to read the full documents.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a summary sheet of a hundred RFCs. You can read it to find out what is in each one without reading all hundred memos.

sections.title: Protocol Standards and Specifications
sections.content: The RFCs from 900 to 999 include important protocol standards and specifications. RFC 998 describes NETBLT, a bulk data transfer protocol. RFC 997 documents Internet Numbers (network numbers and autonomous system numbers). RFC 996 specifies a Statistics Server protocol. RFC 995 and RFC 994 are ISO standards for routing exchange and connectionless network service. RFC 993 discusses PCMAIL, a distributed mail system for personal computers. RFC 991 identifies official ARPA-Internet protocols. RFC 990 documents assigned numbers in protocols. RFC 989 proposes privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail with message encipherment and authentication. RFC 988 specifies host extensions for IP multicasting. RFC 987 describes mapping between X.400 and RFC-822 mail systems. RFC 986 proposes guidelines for using Internet-IP addressing with ISO connectionless-mode network protocol. RFC 985 summarizes requirements for Internet gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: This hundred RFCs includes specifications for many different protocols: ways to transfer big files fast, mail security, multicasting, gateways, and lots of other technical standards.

sections.title: Routing, Gateway, and Network Protocols
sections.content: Multiple RFCs in this range address network routing and gateway topics. RFC 981 describes an experimental multiple-path routing algorithm using wiretap algorithms for packet-radio broadcast channels. RFC 975 proposes enhancements to the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) supporting multiple-level routing with autonomous confederations. RFC 979 contains PSN end-to-end functional specifications describing changes to the Host-to-PSN interface. RFC 977 specifies the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) for distribution and posting of news articles. RFC 976 documents UUCP mail interchange format standards. RFC 973 documents domain system changes and observations, updating earlier DNS specifications. RFC 972 specifies the password generator protocol (PWDGEN) for generating random eight-character pronounceable words.
sections.plainLanguage: These RFCs talk about how data moves between computers: routing protocols that choose the best path, news distribution, mail format standards, and password generation.

sections.title: Experimental and Technical Protocols
sections.content: The range includes several experimental and technical protocols. RFC 992 describes communication support for fault-tolerant process groups. RFC 971 surveys data representation standards including X.409, NBS CBMS, DARPA multimedia mail, Courier RPC, and SUN RPC. RFC 970 explores packet switches with infinite storage and congestion in datagram systems. RFC 969 (obsoleted by RFC 998) described NETBLT. RFC 978 defines the Voice File Interchange Protocol (VFIP) for exchanging speech files. RFC 974 presents mail routing using the domain system and MX resource records. RFC 983 describes ISO transport services on top of TCP, enabling CCITT and ISO session, presentation, and application services on the Internet. RFC 982 provides guidelines for specifying ISO NSAP address structure. RFC 980 indicates how to obtain various protocol documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Some RFCs explore new ideas: moving voice over networks, better ways to represent data, protecting against network congestion, and making ISO services work with the Internet.

sections.title: Historical Status and Obsoletions
sections.content: Several RFCs in the 900-999 range obsolete or update earlier documents, providing a historical record of protocol evolution. RFC 997 (Internet Numbers) obsoletes RFCs 990, 960, 943, 923, and 900, consolidating numbering resources. RFC 998 (NETBLT) obsoletes RFC 969. RFC 991 (Official Protocols) obsoletes RFCs 961, 944, and 924. RFC 993 (PCMAIL) obsoletes RFC 984. This range represents active development in the mid-1980s as the Internet standardized its core infrastructure. The RFCs document both stable standards like IP and TCP and experimental research areas like voice transmission, multicasting, and multipath routing. By publishing RFC 999 as a summary, the community provided a snapshot of the state of standardization through RFC 999, which was itself almost immediately superseded by RFC 1000, which extended the summary to cover all RFCs from 1 to 999.
sections.plainLanguage: These hundred RFCs show how the Internet was developing in 1985-1987. Some are official standards, some replace older standards, and some are experimental ideas that might not work. RFC 999 summarized them all, but then RFC 1000 came along and did it even better.
